review_text_raw:
I'll say it straight, I am not a hacker or an expert programmer, although I had a minimal use of console clients and some programming basics, beside using consoles like DOS in my very first PCs. Hacknet is a hacking game entirely done through console commands and minimal interface in a fictional OS, you'll join tasks to do to go through a main story and a few side jobs, most of the game is all about typing codes on console, the faster you go the better you hack, there are just a few times you must stop and think how to proceed to get the informations or files you need, which is nothing impossible for a beginner. I liked this game for it's way to be different, not too difficult to learn, not too far from reality. 


[b][u]PROS[/u][/b]
[list]

[*][u]HACKING[/u]: There's not much space for hacking effects, beside a few simple animations, hacking goes all through a console, and that's the way real hackers work! The way it makes you feel is great, with some basic commands you can do anything you want without being an IT expert, actually teaching one thing or two about real hacking and consoles! I enjoyed this version of hacking better than unrealistic interactive ways from other games, thumbs up!

[*][u]DIFFICULTY[/u]: Difficulty is very balanced, at least for someone with my experience, it's all about learning a dozen commands, understand what they do and use them for your purposes, not too hard, neither too easy. Once you understand how to use them, you need to get faster and use logic to find what you need, which could be a hidden file or password, beginners shouldn't have too many problems, intermediates woul enjoy it, experts maybe would find it a bit too easy and boring.

[*][u]MINIMAL[/u]: Its minimal graphics just plays a good role, real hackers don't use animations and such, leaving it minimal gives it some realism and fashion, plus makes the game lighter. Thanks for leaving it as minimal as it would be in real hacking, with just very few add ons.

[*][u]STORY AND BACKSTORY[/u]: At first I had the feeling it was short and easy...and I was right, although the climax near the end was awesome, got me stuck into knowing the ending of it and hack into the very last hard tasks, I had to change my opinion about the story, it was good and interesting! There's a bit of backstory about the making of the game, explained by the developer himself, which makes the game's finale even better.

[*][u]WORKSHOP[/u]: I noticed the workshop is enabled and has extra missions and stories to download and play. I admit I didn't try anything from the workshop yet, but sounds like you can expand your game with some addons, which compensaty the main story's shortness and the game's price.

[*][u]SMOOTH AND LIGHT[/u]: Being mostly on console and so minimal, the game runs great on PC with very low hardware requirement. As far as the gameplay experience and fun are untouched, it's a good strong point to distribute the game to low end and PCs not made for gaming.


[/list]


[b][u]CONS[/u][/b]
[list]

[*][u]EYE BOILING[/u]: I've spent about 23 years in front of screens, starting from old CRTs, despite that I never had problems with my sight, either glasses or hurting eyes for long times. Despite that, Hacknet was the first and only game to give me eye pain, not fully sure if my sight is just failing or had a tiring day, but it never happened before. Watching the console for a few hours was a lot worse than I ever experienced before. So be careful, you may need some eye resting from time to time or just not play it for too long.

[*][u]END MISSION EMAILS[/u]: Just like real tasks, you don't win as soon as you reach your objective, most of times you need to send an email back to the contact and it will say if you completed your mission or not. Some tasks requires to write a password in the reply, that way you know what you need to find and what you need to write, but most of times it's all about sending a blank email back, if you didn't complete it, you'll get an error while trying to send the email. To cut it short, there are times you just need to access to files or servers and then answer the email, sometimes your objective is not so clear, so you will get stuck in the email before you fry your mind thinking about stuff you may have skipped or fry the game by reading a step-by-step guide, which kills the fun from the game. There were a few times that frustrated me, maybe giving more informations about the task or send back an email to give hints about the missing tasks would have been better.

[*][u]STORY LENGTH[/u]: Even if short and simple, I praised the story for its climax, but I can't hide a bit of disappointment for being so short, about 9-12 hours for the story, 3-4 extra hours to complete achievements and the other contracts and about 3-4 hours for the DLC (which I don't own nor tried). would have been perfect to almost double its time to make the game truly worth its price, but at least the workshop should help a bit more.

[/list]

Final word: Not too easy, not too hard, made for newbies curious about hacking and people with a bit of knowledge about it. If you accept the compromise to "play" on the console only, it will give you a true hacking feeling and about 10 hours of fun, and I loved it. Recommended for those people, especially if you can find it for a good price!

Just... bad. For anyone remotely familiar with computers, this game is cringe-worthy at best. Some weird mix of unix and dos idioms that just don't exist anywhere. The shell is half-assed and inconsistent, and absolutely nothing even closely emulates the real tools which have had their names disgraced. This game might be decent if the file system behaved the way it should, but it does not. In particular:

- there is no file management beyond rm, mv, and a unicorn scp? can't make directories or copy files on localhost
- devs don't appear to understand how file systems work: ~ and / are used interchangably through the game/tutorial/help docs

some other things to note:
- connections to other systems just don't make sense
- cracking ssh is somehow easier/less resource intensive than screwing with an ftp server? what?
- cat to read files?? really? I smell cat abuse
- no echo?

try again... or don't?

review_text_raw:
I’m not entirely sure what to think about this game. I feel like this game had the potential to be a lot more interesting than it turned out to be. I did have fun with this game and thought some of the missions were interesting. But, I can’t really figure out what this game is trying to be and I came away with the feeling that this game isn’t really finished. 

In terms of hacking and the operating system, it’s fairly weak and, at times, frustrating. The hacking programs you run are basically magic in terms of how powerful they are. They work on anything and require no modification based on the target. The challenge comes from managing your bizarre computer’s memory system and timing attacks to avoid the hollywood-style ‘tracing’. The simplified hacking mechanics aren’t a bad thing, I think. Real hacking elements would make the game extremely complicated, tedious, and boring. 

But, that aside, there are weird limitations on what you can do and what exists in the world. The operating system commands you run are unix-based, but quickly get frustrating to use for anyone familiar with *nix command lines. Autocompletion and wildcards are inconsistent (‘rm *’ works but not ‘rm file_*’). There is no cp (copy), mkdir, rmdir, rsync, or recursion-supported operations. There isn’t even a text editor of any kind, opting for a bizarre ‘replace’ to replace strings in a given file. This just causes more frustration than anything as folders become cluttered and basic OS actions can't be done.

As for the world, hacking into servers and snooping around is fun… to a point. You can read other people’s emails, deface websites, and steal files, which is fun! Then you realize that most of the files you discover are copy-pasted bash.org quotes or filler files which you can’t do anything with. Also, you’re strongly told early on to remove the log files you leave behind when hacking a server, but I’ve yet to find an instance where there are any consequences for not doing so outside of one mission. Finally, and probably my biggest problem, is that you’re pretty much the only active user on the entire internet. You’ll never accidentally encounter another hacker when breaking into a server and you’ll (with one exception) never find log files or evidence of dynamic activity from anyone else on the internet. The world is completely static, apart from a few scripted events. Maybe if there were random encounters or events with other hackers where both of you have the ability to hack each other and other servers, the world wouldn’t feel so static and empty and it would keep you on your toes a bit more. 

The investigation and puzzle aspects of the game are interesting. But, the large number of typos,  grammar mistakes (not sure if these two are intentional or not), and questionable writing can be distracting and confusing. That said, I still had fun. There are times where the missions can be very interesting and even disturbing. And, occasionally, there are times where you have to be clever to solve a puzzle or find a missing piece of information. But, those events are far and few in between. Most of the ‘contracts’ start to feel tedious pretty quickly.

I hate that there is no option inbetween the thumbs up and down, because I think the game is still fun. But, comparing how much I liked to how much I didn’t like, I have to give it a thumbs down. This game has great ideas, it just hasn’t fleshed them out enough.

They work on anything and require no modification based on the target. The challenge comes from managing your bizarre computer’s memory system and timing attacks to avoid the hollywood-style ‘tracing’. The simplified hacking mechanics aren’t a bad thing, I think. Real hacking elements would make the game extremely complicated, tedious, and boring. But, that aside, there are weird limitations on what you can do and what exists in the world. The operating system commands you run are unix-based, but quickly get frustrating to use for anyone familiar with *nix command lines. Autocompletion and wildcards are inconsistent (‘rm *’ works but not ‘rm file_*’). There is no cp (copy), mkdir, rmdir, rsync, or recursion-supported operations. There isn’t even a text editor of any kind, opting for a bizarre ‘replace’ to replace strings in a given file. This just causes more frustration than anything as folders become cluttered and basic OS actions can't be done. As for the world, hacking into servers and snooping around is fun… to a point. You can read other people’s emails, deface websites, and steal files, which is fun! Then you realize that most of the files you discover are copy-pasted bash.org quotes or filler files which you can’t do anything with. Also, you’re strongly told early on to remove the log files you leave behind when hacking a server, but I’ve yet to find an instance where there are any consequences for not doing so outside of one mission. Finally, and probably my biggest problem, is that you’re pretty much the only active user on the entire internet. You’ll never accidentally encounter another hacker when breaking into a server and you’ll (with one exception) never find log files or evidence of dynamic activity from anyone else on the internet. The world is completely static, apart from a few scripted events. Maybe if there were random encounters or events with other hackers where both of you have the ability to hack each other and other servers, the world wouldn’t feel so static and empty and it would keep you on your toes a bit more. The investigation and puzzle aspects of the game are interesting. But, the large number of typos, grammar mistakes (not sure if these two are intentional or not), and questionable writing can be distracting and confusing. That said, I still had fun. There are times where the missions can be very interesting and even disturbing. And, occasionally, there are times where you have to be clever to solve a puzzle or find a missing piece of information. But, those events are far and few in between. Most of the ‘contracts’ start to feel tedious pretty quickly. I hate that there is no option inbetween the thumbs up and down, because I think the game is still fun. But, comparing how much I liked to how much I didn’t like, I have to give it a thumbs down. This game has great ideas, it just hasn’t fleshed them out enough.

review_text_raw:
The game design works at first, and there are timed missions when you really get into the action – musics do their job. You have kind of a sense of accomplishment as you get your hands on more "hacking" tools and get to face bigger challenges. There is quite a lot of humorous content on the side – not in the main story! – and that's appreciated because it's not far from being a text game.

But that's about all the nice things I can think about this game. Pretty soon, you reach its limits and the sense of accomplishment fades away. If you have no feeling for IT stuff, you may get lost pretty fast. But if you're too much into it, the game mechanisms are very disappointing. The main idea was good, but the execution rather bad. If you're still curious, I'd suggest to buy it on sale.

The difficulty relies on: 1. The cryptic aspect of computers – you'd better know the basics about file system and console ;  2. Timed challenges ; 3. Finding little bits of information (user name, password, IP...) here and there among text in files and mail ; 4. Systematically scan the targets in all ways possible. That's not something that keeps one entertained for long.

The console, which you use a lot, is rather rudimentary. At the very least it should have felt like a real one and at least to go smoothly when you type. The cursor is glitchy, not always showing where it actually is. Key pushes may be repeated when hold a few microseconds too long. The number of commands is very limited. They are sometimes buggy when not used as intended. Managing the in-game files is pretty tedious, there are no commands for creating/deleting directories. There is no way to make scripts or shortcuts. At best you can rename the executables. By the way, having "exe" files on a Linux simulation is an heresy.

The graphic interface lacks functionalities too. It would be great if you could move and resize the panels, especially the one for the "netmap" which gets pretty packed and hard to read after a while. You may find an in-game executable which helps a little bit with that. Also content will overflow from panels when too big. Why no copy/paste available?!? It would have been so useful. I grew tired of retype every user name, password and IP. Plus there are some links that are meant to be open in a real browser (as eater eggs only).

The game mechanisms are very limited. Some special missions or events break the monotony, but the player are not prepared for them either. [spoiler]For instance you are not likely to be able to defend your computer against other hackers.[/spoiler] The hacking tools are also limited in number, in versions and they almost all work in the same way. Missions are quite alike, and you're doing the same dull things over, and over, and over...

They tried to make up for it with the game story, but it turns out to be a bit déjà vu, corny, and even a bit predictable.

Two alternatives would have been preferable for making such a game:
— Either make it more approachable, even less realistic but with a more pleasant game design. Then it would need hacking to be more like puzzles.
— Or make a game for nerds, where the in-game computers can be configured, where files matter, with better console commands and executables, even maybe some scripts to edit.

review_text_raw:
This is, perhaps, one of the stranger games I've ever played, but I'm totally glad that I did. As you begin cracking into systems you end up meeting with some pretty enjoyable dilemmas and puzzles. Even after cracking every system in the vanilla game, with 3 unique and interesting stories to follow for great replay value, I still find myself coming back to this game just to play through again and again. 

At first, I wasn't sure if I would enjoy a "terminal-based" game, starting with very little knowledge beyond old DoS systems, but the game walks you through it in a comfortable pace that's easy to learn with a little bit of practice and a little bit of /help. The story is immersive and the UI is actually kind of impressive, especially for leaving up in a domain control room at work! ;)
This was the first game that, while still definitely a little bit of a fantasy world, actually looked and felt a little bit like real hacking.

review_text_raw:
This is a fun little game, Unix terminal knowledge is useful but not required beyond the basics. If you're the sort of person who enjoys fiddling around in other people's shit surrupticiously this is your game. If you do happen to know some Unix stuff, a lot of common real-world terminal programs alias to actual game features (like less aliases to cat for reading text files for example). The hacking minigame part is fairly simple and the "memory" mechanic is a clever way of making you have to think ahead.

If I had one request, it'd be to implement rudimentary Bash and shell scripting as well as build in a little more junk that requires thinking to manage (ex. more dummy processes when invoking ps). Or maybe it's already there and I'm just not far enough into the game yet. Also file management needs a little work, my /home is a fuckin mess after just invoking scp * in every folder on every system I come through. Either way, good fun.

For those on the fence, one of the first "real" jobs you get is stealing Centucky Fried Chicken's secret recipe. I am become Hackerman.

review_text_raw:
[b]Hacknet[/b] is a hacking simulation game. You are probably familiar with other games of the same genre, such as Uplink and the Hacker Evolution series. This game is, I dare to say, better than both of those, despite having some bugs.
If this review is too long for you, I suggest you to only read the first paragraph about the game's content and the final verdict at the end.

[h1] What is happening in the game: [/h1]
Fourteen days after Agent Bit's disappearance, a failsafe sequence was activated. You are one of the only people who can solve Bit's death. As you get more and more involved into the hacker community, you start unveiling a mystery and it's up to you to discover what was really behind Bit and the security system he created.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*]After the success of Uplink, there had to be a game sooner or later that would try to improve what Uplink started. Hacknet not only achieves that, but takes it to the next level. The story alone is amazing and makes sure that you're not just repeating the same commands and actions over and over but gives it a meaning.
[*]I have to say that the whole interface is working really nicely when it comes to clarity and effectiveness. You can do 90% of things both in the Display section and Terminal section, but they are both placed in the interface and I find it surprisingly effective. I use the Display section for figuring out what is going on and the Terminal section to execute commands.
[*]You have a nice map on the bottom of the screen, that is showing all of the cyber locations you have visited already. As you get to connect to tons of computers, you would think that the map would be overcrowded, but this is not the case. I found the map really useful, despite it being almost completely covered.
[*]There is no bouncing from servers as you remember from other hacking games. Instead, traces are lost if you simply disconnect. Even better is the way how the developers managed what happens if you get traced. Your computer (the virtual one, of course) activates a failsafe sequence. It tells you the IP of your ISP and your IP. You have to break into your ISP's server in a very limited amount of time and from there, reset your IP. This is a brilliant way to prevent accidental game overs and having to start all over again. Instead, you are provided with one more hard (and fun) challenge.
[*]I really enjoy the soundtrack in this game. The song was written by a guy who also made the soundtrack for Hotline Miami. The music matches with the tension of your current illegal doings and really makes your heart beat faster. Amazing job.
[*]The in-game hacking is based on actual UNIX commands, which is pretty cool. Still, don't expect to be a pro hacker when you finish this game. You would still be a few steps away, the first step being stopping playing hacking simulators instead of learning the real deal.
[*]There is a ton of Easter Eggs in this game. A clicker game, hidden Steam keys and a lot more. [*]It's really impressive how they manage to fit all sorts of things into this game. Also, you should read all of the IRC chat logs when you encounter them. They can be super funny (and useful).
[*]I have cooperated with the developer in bug-related issues and I have to say that I really like the way that the developer interacts with the community. (Almost) all of the bugs I have encountered were fixed and I'm glad that they managed to bring the final release in a shape that they did.
[*]Another interesting aspect of this game is puzzle solving. You have to think really hard to solve some of them and you even have to remember things from your previous missions, write things down and stuff like that.
[*]If you don't like the user interface, you will encounter skins later in the game that you can download and make your virtual computer looks just the way you want.
[*]The system requirements are low, which is great for old computers. However, there are some moments when FPS suddenly drops and gets to a normal level quickly.
[*]$/€10 is a steal for a game of such quality. If you ever enjoyed hacking games, this should be the top game on your wishlist.

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
Bugs. Many were fixed, but some are still present. The game-breaking ones are gone, however, so you should be fine.
This game should have a button to reset progress. I wanted to do that a couple of times but you can't really do that without browsing through folders and files.

[h1]The final verdict:[/h1]
As a big fan of hacking games, I was very happy to be able to play Hacknet. The game is certainly made well and definitely recommend this game to you if you enjoy hacking games as well. The story is surprisingly good and adds an important part to the whole experience. The hacking really feels real and, even though that the commands are pretty much the same through the whole game, never feel repetitive.
This is, no doubt, the best hacking game ever released. Get it, and fast!

This was Kedeajan,
Have fun!
dc

review_text_raw:
*Got the game for $2.99 during a sale*

Hacknet is an interesting game. Let's just get that out of the way. Its got a very good storyline and, while I have some experience in [strike]hacking[/strike] computer security, I didn't find (most) of the puzzles too difficult for the average person to solve. It sets a very good pace, picking up the difficulty very well. I'm writing this review just after completing the game, which took me just over 6 hours.

You start off with a message from Bit, telling you how to use the Hacknet software, etc. etc. Basically a tutorial on how to use it, the command line, that sort of thing. (If you're a linux user, this game will be much easier, the commands are basically the same for navigating the terminal and the like) After this, you're sent off to a hacker group, Entropy. You do a few hacks, and things start to pick up. You rise to the top (naturally) and start going off, investigating. I'd say more but I don't want to risk spoilers. The ending was very intriguing, and worth the effort.

The challenges are similar, but I never got bored of them. Find server at X IP, break down any proxies, firewalls, and open ports to use the almighty PortHack and get the admin password. Then, do whatever you need to, be it uploading or downloading a file, deleting stuff, or (later) even messing with databases and some... other devices. ([spoiler]a pacemaker[/spoiler]) They become more difficult as you progress, adding tracers that initiate an IP change failsafe if you take too long, more ports to open, and more complex firewalls and proxies. You'll need to grab passwords from emails and circumvent servers with powerful tracers, and even more interesting events. The only randomly difficult challenge that jumped me was an attack on my PC, which I was able to avoid using a [spoiler]trap shell[/spoiler]. If it gets you, there is a guide to help you out.

The interface is very intuitive and I never had any unreasonable issues with it, aside from becoming stuck when entering a password I didn't want to enter. (Which is my fault, I clicked login. What did I expect?) Later, you get the option to switch your layout, but none of them are really terrible. You have the terminal window (for commands), the display window (for showing the filesystem, passwords, databases, emails, etc.), the RAM window (watch this one, especially later when you get more RAM-hungry programs), and your NetMap (showing all the IPs you've connected to/can connect to).

The playtime was a good length. I would have liked it to be a bit longer but 6 hours is longer than AAA campaigns. God I hate AAA companies. Be innovative. Or I'll use Hacknet to take down your servers. /rant. Anyway, I'm not complaining about the length. As I said earlier, it never got repetitive, it was always interesting. There was always a sense of "oh gotta do this quickly or they're gonna catch me with that trace" that pushes you forward. Because of that speed though, don't play this game if you're not a quick typist. I have a speed of about 70 WPM (Faster now), which is well above average. I'd recommend being able to go above 40 WPM to play this effectively. 

------------------------------------------------------

Of course, what's a review without a pro/con list.

Pros:
+Good, interesting gameplay
+Active modding community (for extra levels and whatnot)
+Great value for the price (Yes, I know I got it for $2.99. But it's worth the full $9.99)
+Nice visuals (watch out, 1 looks like lowercase L. Tripped me up once)
+Easter Egg bash.org quotes
+Amazing soundtrack. Reflects the mood and urgency of the situations. 10/10 on that.

Neutrals:
+-Console window pops up behind game (Alt Tabbing is a little wierd)
+-Can't skip ending credits

Cons:
-You need to be a quick and accurate typist
-Requires some prior knowledge of terminal commands in order to be efficient (from the start)

------------------------------------------------------

TL; DR

Very interesting, non-repetitive gameplay and a good storyline. Visuals are of high quality and the soundtrack is amazing. However, to be good at this game you should be good at typing ( >40 WPM) and know how to navigate the Linux terminal, or at least pick up on it quickly. (I mean, it's just ls, cd, cat, and mv really) Also, bash.org quotes.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
UPDATE
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

I've just finished the Hacknet: Labyrinths DLC. I'm adding a short little note here about that.

Definetely worth it. Took an extra 3 and a half hours or so to complete, so pretty decent playtime. Much more interesing puzzles than the base game. You are tasked with completing the "Kaguya Trials" from the CSEC list, and join with a group of 3 other hackers. You'll take missions from a list and complete them with the help of the others. While you usually never actually interact with them other than seeing them in the IRC, it does feel like they're helping you. (I won't spoil how, but it becomes apparent in the endgame.) The challenges were a bit more difficult, but nothing that wasn't impossible. A mission towards the end just becomes a cat-and-mouse chase for a password, but while it didn't seem to guide you it wasn't that difficult to follow the clues. Overall, I'd highly rate the DLC. If you have the extra cash when buying Hacknet, I would recommend purchasing it. Do complete it after the main game though, or your NetMap will become a mess...

------------------------------------------------------

TL; DR

Very well done game and a great expansion to the original. I would definitely recommend purchasing this alongside the base game. Just... Play it after you beat the base game.

review_text_raw:
1. You can't finish all contracts. At some point the game will just tell you "You're good enough for more difficult tasks" and a main quest will trigger, blocking you from accepting new quests. You can never go back and you can't do them after the final mission.

2. You can't create files or directories. Organizing your downloaded files is annoying because you can only use the pre-defined ones. In one contract you're supposed to forge a file, and that works by downloading a file and editing the copy...

3. You can't remove directories. There's almost never a need to do so, but when you need to remove the contents from a directory with multiple subdirectories, you need to access each subdir individually and remove the contents.

4. Autocomplete doesn't add a whitespace after the autocompleteted word. Confusing as hell for a regular terminal user.

5. The final mission consists of multiple phases, which each one explaining your next goal. In phase 3 you're supposed to send a password but you aren't told so. I just used the password I found to login and continued my quest. After a while I got stuck, and after more than an hour I finally looked into a walkthrough - and learnt that I needed to send the password instead of entering it, and that had already solved the final mission by myself over an hour ago. At least I could just click the "complete quest" button 4 times in a row to trigger the ending.

6. The gameplay is quite repetetive. Connect to a server, open the closed ports (which always works the same, for all of them), find the file you need. There are only 2 missions that go beyond that and actually force you to think: The final mission, and the mission before. That doesn't really speak for the game.

7. The map is just plain awful. It's cluttered with nodes from earlier contracts which you never need to connect to anymore. Literally hardest part of the game is finding the correct node on the map.

8. Secrets. Don't get me wrong, secrets are great. But I looked into a guide after finishing the game, and some secrets didn't trigger for me although I definitely satisfied their conditions. So maybe I shouldn't have written "Secrets", but "Bugs". Furthermore, some secrets get you hyped, and when you finally solve their puzzle, you get... a digital clock that even uses up your RAM?

9. Alt+Tab closes the game.

I completed the game in a single session. It was kinda fun, although way too easy. But damn, some of the issues I just mentioned are pissing me off and I'm not going to play the DLC or any user-created mod.

review_text_raw:
Hacknet is a game about hacking. The game opens with the Hacknet OS booting up with a message from a man named Bit, who says that if you see the message, he’s already dead. He leads you on a quest to start hacking, getting the attention of one hacker group, then a second, all to avenge his death and prevent the distribution of a hacking program.

The story itself is kind of mediocre, but it is serviceable; at its core, it is a story of corporate greed, as well as a revenge story, though by the end of it, it is pretty clear that the whole thing isn’t really as sinister as it appeared at first.

The real core of the story is the hacking – you log into various computers, break through their security mechanisms, and then are lead onto other computers. Spicing things up are timers, various mechanisms you have to bypass, and the various files and passwords and IPs you have to find to lead you on the next leg of your hunt.

Sadly, the game is plagued with poor design decisions. There are various points at which it isn’t clear what you’re supposed to be doing, and you’re left confused, only to find out you needed to hit the “reply” button on an email after breaking into a server to move on – despite the fact that the email wasn’t clear about that. At other times, you have to send them messages, and while this is usually clear (sending them an IP or password), on occasion it is not and ends up being rather frustrating.

Worse (and even more frustrating) are some outright bugs – situations where the game simply does not function like it is supposed to. Beyond there being some lost forevers in the game which are less than obvious, there’s additionally the fact that sometimes the game simply bugs out and won’t let you progress or do various things. You get a “mission incomplete” message when trying to proceed, and there’s simply no clear way around the issue. Indeed, two of the achievements require you to do things which simply don’t function half the time or more, judging by the many frustrated players who had to restart the game time and again to try and get them to work.

The UI itself is a bit obtuse at times as well; several of the hacking programs you use require additional bits of typing to execute, despite the fact that in many cases it literally never matters – it is always exactly the same number you have to punch in. And while it is neat seeing it use actual hackerish commands, ultimately there’s a lot of little pieces which just feel annoying to have to do time and again.

The only real good thing about the game is its aesthetics; which do work pretty well for what it is.

In the end, you aren’t really rewarded for your frustration. The core idea is cute enough, but in the end the game ends up being rather repetitive, and there just isn’t enough variation in the core gameplay. A mediocre story combined with sometimes unclear gating mechanics to make the game advance is just not a winning recipe for a game.

The game seems like a neat idea at first, but it just ends up being more frustrating than enjoyable to play. It isn’t worth your time or your money.

For those who have touched a terminal or command prompt, or even for those that never have but want to, give this game a go. It starts off quick and simple with lots of tools, tips and plenty of time that you need to get comfortable working in a terminal. As long as you learn how to navigate file directories and read any .txt you find, it's worthwhile to vibe out and do whatever you want, then do the tasks you need when you're ready.

Re: Steam Deck, this is one of those games that heavily rely on the keyboard. While the native runtime of this game works well (no Proton required), you need a keyboard connected to your Deck to have a good experience. It's nice playing a story-driven puzzle title like this on the Deck's small screen, but docked at a desk is most optimal. Just in case, map the Deck's touchpad to a mouse cursor with Left Click and a scroll wheel to access the on-screen shortcuts without repeatedly typing them; while the Deck' touchscreen can work, it's nice to have a backup way to click around.

review_text_raw:
HACKNET - 7/10

Quick Review: A "hacking simulator" with gameplay akin to getting your first DOS system up and running, Hacknets weak story doesn't hold back the interesting and ever expanding gameplay.

Story
------
You, an amateur hacker, are contacted by someone named "Bit", who gives you an extra tool to add to your hacking repertoire and from there the expansive world is open to you. Using your new found tools, you become a part of something greater, helping (obviously shady) people with your hacking skills while trying to figure out just what the hell the Hacknet really is, and it might be more dangerous than you thought...

Overall, unfortunately the story is the weakest point. Everything is told through text in the game and the story really only starts to open up and become explained by the end but by that time you're more than likely burnt out from your constant reading. Most of the game has you completing irrelevant odd jobs for obvious scum with little relevance to the story, which is why the story is the weakest part.

Gameplay
-----------
Gameplay of Hacknet involves 2 things: typing and hacking. Your UI is a command window with a display of the target computer in the center, all the devices you have access to at the bottom and the command console on the right. Basic gameplay goes like this: Select a PC you want to hack, you "probe" it (by typing "probe") which will display a list of security measures. You then type whatever relevant command you need for the security measure (theres about 6 different types and you'll get the tools required as you progress through the game), wait a bit for it to be hacked, than do whatever it is the quest needs you to do; either copy a file to your system, delete a file, edit a file, find an ip address and send it to the client etc. The entire game revolves around typing commands and clicking files.

I do think the gameplay is fun however, it has to be for me to give it a 7/10. By the time you get the hang of your newly introduced command, you'll learn yet another and another until you get near the end. There is alot you can do and quite alot of secrets to find as you make your way through the story. The gameplay at it's core is simple but it takes a while to memorise all the power you have.

Design
-------
The UI for the game is great, and the gameplay experience really makes you feel like H4CK3RM@NZ.  You get access to different coloured themes as you progress, and alot of the files you can find on the computers are quite hilarious. The soundtrack is a banger too, and the end of the game features some of the best final music i've ever heard.

Problems
----------
It's a simple game, so it has simple problems. Alot of the text files you find on computers are just copy pasted across many devices, filling them up so you spend more time browsing through them than needed. There was a bit too much waiting involved when it came to hacking and required almost 0 thought, you simply type the command for whatever hacking tool you need and the number that corresponds with it, then you wait. The biggest problem I have is that as you get further and further in the game, the amount of devices you can access starts to clutter your device map. Because devices are represented as circles with no names, I spent ages hovering over 30+ circles trying to find what computer I was looking for, and they end up overlapping sometimes too. This sometimes made me have to re-hack into a previous computer to find the IP for the computer I wanted to hack into even if I already had it available, simply because it was impossible to find on my device map.

Achievements
---------------
The achievements are....relatively easy and can be gotten in 1 playthrough but you need to know what to do without the game telling you. You need to discover quite a few secrets and go out of your way to get alot of the achievements but there isn't an enormous amount of content in the game so as long as you try and explore everything you'll probably get them.

Summary
----------
A super unique experience and nothing like i've ever played. The banging soundtrack and addictive gameplay makes me easily recommend this, but only if you can overlook it's numerous, but not awful problems.

Also I can't stress enough the end of the game. It's seriously, SERIOUSLY amazing and worth playing just to experience it. Everything about it is great and the song that plays alongside it couldn't have been more perfect...for anything.

review_text_raw:
It's possible that HackNet is the most fun I've had in a LONG LONG time.    At first, I thought it was a little hokey.. Sort of like how Hollywood movies portray hacking.. And then as the plot develops (closer to the end), everything started to fit into place... The overdone interfaces, the limited options... everything...  slotted together... perfectly..

OK, so this game is pretty much for geeks and programming/unix nerds.  If you've never used a command prompt, and think typing your username into the PSN login is "programming", this ain't for you.   This game relies on an X-Server-like interface, and relies on fast typing, and a fair working knowledge of what a server is, ports, IP Addresses, and so on. Knowing that you can press "up" in a shell window to get to previously typed commands, for instance, can save a lot of typing.. It's that kind of knowledge which comes in handy...

The game presents itself as an X-server interface with a fixed layout (which can be modified in-game!), you just can't drag windows about. You wouldn't want to, anyway.  The layout is perfect for what you need.   There's a "net map" to show your progress, a terminal for typing in commands, and an all-purpose web-browser interface.

You have control of an advanced unix-based OS which has serious MIL-spec hacking software installed on it.  The server comes with an timed message, which asks you to perform 'a favour' for the previous owner of the software...  And from that point on, you're sucked headfirst into the screen, as you probe, hack, and trace your way around the internet.

You're not alone, though.  There's a few groups out there who do this sort of thing every day of the week.  Some of them are REALLY good.  But all of them are using old-gen kit, so while you know next-to-nothing, you're already as powerful as the best of them... With a little training, and some experience, you can be the best Hacker on the 'Net... 

The game is about 50% hacking simulation (a-la Hollywood) with flashy graphics, and fast, heart-pounding music to crank up the tension.   You have to 'connect' to a server to inject cracks and exploits onto it.  Once running, you can disconnect from the server and let them run.  As long as you're connected, you're vulnerable to being traced and back-hacked!   But if you disconnect too often or too quickly, you may need to start over.  It's a brilliant device which deviates slightly from accepted terminology, but works great as a game device.    The other 50% of the game is done after you've successfully breached a server.  Your OS filters out all the unnecessary stuff, leaving you with the important bits.. And buried in that dross are gold nuggets.. Usernames, passwords, blackmail material, recipes (sic), saved IRC quotes, and all-important IP addresses to other servers.  

Once you hook up with a team of other hackers, you can opt to take on 'contracts' to hack into servers to perform tasks.  Some of them require you to figure out where you have to hack, and might involve chain-hacks of three or four servers.  Each one holds the key (somewhere) to the next (you hope), or might be a dead-end to slow you down....  Who knows? The game randomizes some element each playthrough, so you may never be 100% sure!

As you get better, you may find your current group is pretty small-fry, or doesn't take the sorts of things you want to.. you may want to move up in the world....  But all the time, at the back of your mind... Who was the previous owner of this awesome system?  Am I the only one with it?  who else has it?  Why can I run Windows .EXEs on a *nix box?!?!    Perhaps you'll get to find out....

Partway through the game, there's a mini-easter egg which spawns a nice little side-plot.  You can continue on through without triggering it.. But once you win the game, there's a (sort-of) hint about how to trigger it.. but TBH, just go read the forums.    The side-plot is short, sweet, and switches things up a bit.

I loved the variety in the game.   It's amazing, because (at its core) everything is the same... A circle with an IP address, that exposes ports, and may be protected...  But how you get that circle varies... And what that circle entails varies...   The logs, emails, and text files throughout the game paint a glorious picture (with many spelling mistakes!),  giving you a grand idea of the people at the other end of the pipe.

From the first moment I started this game, I loved every second of it.  When I was away from the PC, I was trying to think   a) how I could solve the puzzle I was stuck at   and  b) how I could get back to the PC to play it...

In-game explanation is fair.  Actually figuring out what you have to do is relatively straightforward:  It generally boils down to executing a particular command to attempt to breach a particular piece of security.   The in-game explanation, however, makes it sound a little more complicated than it is.  Just read it through, and try the commands out.

I phreaking loved this game.  It was AWESOME.  I can't wait for the expansion to come out later in 2016!

You have to 'connect' to a server to inject cracks and exploits onto it. Once running, you can disconnect from the server and let them run. As long as you're connected, you're vulnerable to being traced and back-hacked! But if you disconnect too often or too quickly, you may need to start over. It's a brilliant device which deviates slightly from accepted terminology, but works great as a game device. The other 50% of the game is done after you've successfully breached a server. Your OS filters out all the unnecessary stuff, leaving you with the important bits.. And buried in that dross are gold nuggets.. Usernames, passwords, blackmail material, recipes (sic), saved IRC quotes, and all-important IP addresses to other servers. Once you hook up with a team of other hackers, you can opt to take on 'contracts' to hack into servers to perform tasks. Some of them require you to figure out where you have to hack, and might involve chain-hacks of three or four servers. Each one holds the key (somewhere) to the next (you hope), or might be a dead-end to slow you down.... Who knows? The game randomizes some element each playthrough, so you may never be 100% sure! As you get better, you may find your current group is pretty small-fry, or doesn't take the sorts of things you want to.. you may want to move up in the world.... But all the time, at the back of your mind... Who was the previous owner of this awesome system? Am I the only one with it? who else has it? Why can I run Windows .EXEs on a *nix box?!?! Perhaps you'll get to find out.... Partway through the game, there's a mini-easter egg which spawns a nice little side-plot. You can continue on through without triggering it.. But once you win the game, there's a (sort-of) hint about how to trigger it.. but TBH, just go read the forums. The side-plot is short, sweet, and switches things up a bit. I loved the variety in the game. It's amazing, because (at its core) everything is the same... A circle with an IP address, that exposes ports, and may be protected... But how you get that circle varies... And what that circle entails varies... The logs, emails, and text files throughout the game paint a glorious picture (with many spelling mistakes!), giving you a grand idea of the people at the other end of the pipe. From the first moment I started this game, I loved every second of it. When I was away from the PC, I was trying to think a) how I could solve the puzzle I was stuck at and b) how I could get back to the PC to play it... In-game explanation is fair. Actually figuring out what you have to do is relatively straightforward: It generally boils down to executing a particular command to attempt to breach a particular piece of security. The in-game explanation, however, makes it sound a little more complicated than it is. Just read it through, and try the commands out. I phreaking loved this game. It was AWESOME. I can't wait for the expansion to come out later in 2016!

review_text_raw:
This game is good. Just not great.

I actually didn't finish this game, but I read a story synopsis and it was, well, not too creative. Decent, but not amazing. The reason I didn't finish is because the story effectively takes a break for about 8-10 hours after the first hour, having you invest into smaller stories that you come across in small missions. The other reason I didn't finish was that the gameplay felt like actual hacking and work, and it was the kind of grindy, difficult work that one might receive in a classroom. Some features of the UI were extremely difficult to operate, and while that was somewhat realistic, I came to play a game, not because I liked doing difficult computer work, which is part of the reason why some hackers become hackers. Speaking of that, this game makes hacking extremely easy and simplified. I guess that if a hacking OS was developed in real life, it may actually be this easy, but in reality now hacking is way more difficult, complicated and sometimes more fun than this.

The world building and details were fantastic. I can't tell you how many times I laughed scrolling through logs on PCs I'd hacked into. They were well written and funny. But the massive break from the story made me feel like I was actually doing hacker work (although way too easy) and not playing a game. I came to experience a story, play a game, be something and someone else for a while, not to actually do hacker work. This game did not advertise as a hacker sim, but as a game where you play as a hacker with a story. That is my main problem with this game.

And don't get me wrong--I am all about games that require you do think and reflect and do not have big visuals or explosions or gunfights--this game's gameplay was boring. I've already said how the hacking was too easy and the UI was way too hard, but simply, hacking got boring rather quickly. That's basically it. In terms of additional information, there were no bugs and it was programmed very solidly. 

Overall, get this game when it is very cheap and play it for a few hours. You can have more fun with it than just two hours, so you don't have to return it, just buy it very cheap or free, that's how I got this game, it was free for a limited time and I downloaded it. 79/100 -- good, just not a B.

review_text_raw:
[+] Soundtrack
[+] User Interface

[-] Plot
[-] World design and interaction

I bought this game mainly for its soundtrack, then because I'm a terminal guy myself and I love typing commands.
From this standpoint the game is beautiful: hastily keyboard mashing while listening to Gallego's killer tracks was awesome, not even mentioning the time when Carpenter Brut took over...

This game perfectly sets the mood for an awesome experience, with its music, its terminals and pseudo-graphical GUIs... but then falls short story-side.

[b]The plot is dull, linear and somewhat predictable.[/b]
You only have one bifurcation of the storyline that's even non-obvious to unlock. It gives you access to some more interesting missions, a new faction, and let you see a dark corner of the in-game Internet; but then it merges back into the main path in an abrupt way, as meaningless as it could get.
Yes, there are some interesting easter eggs and strange computer systems, but nothing that makes you want to explore on your own all that much.
There's only, like, [i]one[/i] moral choice, and it's not even part of the main quest.

[b]Whatever you do, whoever you damage, there's no consequence. The world simply doesn't react.[/b]
No cops backtracing you, no factions you can anger, no reputation system: you're part of the Good Guys from start to finish; you can screw up all the machines you want, you are The Savior and no one will change that.
Heck, you can even fail hacks and, apart from a panicking minigame to atone, no officer nor corporate killer will ever knock on your door.
You're simply bounced from a Good faction to another, without any chance to express your will. Just keep on hacking. Don't even bother to cover up your footprints. Logs are useless.

In the end, yes you can buy it, sure, but don't expect much except aesthetics.


[TECHNICAL NOTE]
The in-game console is backed by your native OS, and everything is deeply woven with its runtime.
Yes, you read it right.
That means two things:
[list]
    [*] if some of your game files break, you can be welcomed by an OS error printed on the console;
    [*] while this game runs on both Windows and Linux and has cloud sync, the save files are [b]not[/b] cross-platform; I suspect it has to do with different text encodings (save files are simple XMLs), and you need a repair tool you can find on the forums in order to convert them.
[/list]
Yeah, that wasn't nice.

Hacknet – A Thrilling Hacking Simulation You Should Try!

Ever wondered what it’s like to be a hacker? Hacknet puts you in the role of one, simulating a realistic command-line hacking experience where you’ll breach systems, retrieve and delete files, cover your tracks, and complete secretive missions—all from a simulated computer interface.

The game starts with a tutorial, easing you into the basics of scanning ports, bypassing security, and using various hacking tools. You’ll mainly use the keyboard to type commands, though there are some mouse-friendly options. Typing commands yourself makes it feel even more immersive, like you’re truly hacking into systems.

The first task introduces you to the mechanics by having you break into a system, access files, and erase logs to avoid detection. From there, the game picks up as you receive emails guiding you toward new hacking jobs (which you technically could ignore, but where’s the fun in that?).

If you’re into cyber-thrillers or just love problem-solving, Hacknet is a must-try. It’s engaging, challenging, and makes you feel like a real hacker. Highly recommended!

review_text_raw:
[h1][b]IF YOU LIKE THE IDEA OF A GAME FOCUSING ENTIRELY ON A TERMINAL/COMMAND-LINE AND SOME EASY TO MODERATELY DIFFICULT PUZZLES THROWN IN, YOU MAY LIKE THIS GAME.[/b][/h1]
As someone who has a bit of experience with the UNIX terminal and commands, this game had my absolute full attention and felt familiar to me. [b]I've just recently bought this game (yesterday, at the time of writing) and I was absolutely HOOKED and couldn't get away from it. Hacknet is absolutely my style of game! (right now, I've just beaten the base game and will go through the DLC content shortly. but I may fiddle around with the Extensions)[/b]

[h1][b]TARGET[/b][/h1]
Obviously, this game isn't for everyone. A terminal-based game can seem intimidating or uninteresting to someone who has no experience with it before (and even if you do, a terminal-based game may not be that interesting). If the screenshots and description provided by the game do not capture your attention, it's probably not the game for you. But if your curiosity is piqued, it may be a great experience for you.

[h1][b]PUZZLE ELEMENTS AND TUTORIALS[/b][/h1]
Hacknet introduces itself quite well to the uninformed, and doesn't hand-hold. It throws you straight in after a short tutorial on using the terminal and interface, therefore encouraging experimentation with what you have available. By not holding the player's hand, succeeding in the puzzles without any additional help besides what the game provides will give you a sense of accomplishment. However, that can turn some people off, and if it does, it may not be for you.

It is possible to get stuck in several points in the game, but no solution is too far out there and is solvable without a walkthrough. (and I admit, I have, and have consulted a walkthrough but I was extra careful not to look any further ahead than the current task at hand, most of the time I had just forgotten something simple and was able to get back on track quickly).

The puzzles start off pretty easy, leading you on and increasing the difficulty as it goes, pretty much gently guiding you on how to work with the game's unique nature.

At certain times, the tasks can seem repetitive, and to be fair, it is. You are constantly trying to break into a lot of different computers, servers, devices, etc. but that's what it is. It is an accurate representation instead of the flashy Hollywood style hacking seen on film (but it certainly can be flashy when it wants to be and is for certain parts).

[h1][b]STORY[/b][/h1]
The story itself is nothing outstanding, but it certainly fits the theme and style of the game. It's perfect for the game. The story is there for the beginning and the end of your gameplay, giving you purpose to start and an objective to reach near the end. In the middle of the game, you are given freedom to do what you wish. Or PointClicker, if that's your thing (I won't judge!).

[h1][b]MUSIC[/b][/h1]
The music is an absolute fit for Hacknet and I often found myself focusing on the killer beats rather than what's at hand. It also made me quite shaky during the parts that are time-based.

[h1][b]OVERALL[/b][/h1]
Overall, Hacknet is extremely accurate compared to other things that have tried to display this kind of topic before. The elements work wonderfully and the balance between gameplay and the real elements is on point (all the commands given are used at one point or another and no unnecessary garbage is there). To the average person who may not know anything about the terminal, it can be exciting to get into it for the first time not knowing anything and eventually learn (there may be a little higher risk of getting stuck at a point, but that's okay!). To those who are a little familiar with the terminal and commands, you'll feel right at home and understand the game quickly and have a great time with it!

[h1][b]SHOULD YOU GET IT?[/b][/h1]
If this game looks interesting, [b]IT WILL BE FOR YOU.[/b] The terminal looks intimidating from the start, and if that doesn't deter you and the description of the game brings you in further, you [b]WILL[/b] enjoy it!

review_text_raw:
What a great game. I acquired this in a Humble Bundle recently with a few other titles. Without looking, I assumed it was just a game that was shoveled in to fluff out the bundle, and that I wouldn't enjoy it. I ended up loving it, and I'm definitely going to buy the DLC (and likely any more content that may come out for Hacknet in the future).

Hacknet, for lack of better words, is a Unix-based hacking simulator in which you use the combination of a point-and-click interface and a command prompt to explore the mysterious death of a hacker named "Bit." Bit has arranged to send automated messages to you posthumously, giving you leads that are just enough for you to find your way.

Being not much of a programmer, and unfamiliar with Linux and Unix-based command systems (idk man I just look stuff up and punch shit into the Windows 10 command prompt and sometimes it says words back to me), I felt learning to play Hacknet might be too daunting of a task. However, the feeling subsided in less than half an hour, when I was able to navigate through any device's file systems with ease, hopping from device to device, opening ports, cracking passwords, etc. Not long after that was I very immersed in the story (something I have a hard time being in MANY games).

While some aspects of the game can be done through clicking between devices, folders, and apps, other things are seemingly only possible by using the command-line, keeping the game immersive and making you feel, in a sense, accomplished. YOU cracked open all of Macrosoft's ports and got to snoop around in their sensitive files. YOU found a security loophole by exploiting a computer's connected smartphone. YOU made a clean getaway just in time before having your IP traced, clearing the system logs and running for the hills with some juicy new program you can use to hack *even more* devices. And you did it all with your analytical skills and an intuitive command system. In fact, there's even a point in the game where your OS/interface is essentially deleted from your system by another angry hacker, leaving you with a big black command terminal, having to plot through your own computer to restore the deleted files and get yourself back in the game. Just like in real life, each device you access seems like a sum of its parts, even your own.

The IP tracing mechanic is excellent, and pretty much exactly what you'd imagine seeing on some Hollywood hacker's monitor. It keeps the pressure on, even if it is slow at times. RAM management, learning what ports to use when, and being able to type quickly and remember which programs do what are important, and make hacking into each and every system rewarding in its own way, even if it doesn't have quite what you were looking for.

The visual effects are excellent, if a bit cheesy at times. The interface is simple enough that these "glitchy" or "tech-y" effects aren't too jarring unless they need to be, which keeps the game immersive but also fun to watch. I'd advise that anyone with epilepsy be careful with this game at some times - lots of effects are fast or flashy in nature.

The story doesn't seem to thrust itself into your face at all. Save for the occasional automated (but justified) email from Bit, you discover all of the story on your own, and every lead and new piece of information feels genuine and is worth discovering.

Overall, I had a lot of fun with this game. Two complaints (which end up not really being complaints after I explain them):

- The IP map, showing all known devices and their IPs, can get a bit cluttered, and it's easy to forget where one particular computer is on the big web of spinning circles and lines connecting them. The position of an IP address on the map is not always intuitive. However, this could arguably help with immersion, making you feel like you're navigating through a web of IP addresses. It's the internet in its raw form - not catered to your viewing pleasure.

- I'm left wanting more. Not that I didn't get my money's worth, but I want more. But that's something every game should strive for - leaving you wanting more, and not outstaying its welcome.

Challenging, but *very* rewarding command system that makes you feel clever. Decent story that keeps you invested throughout the game. Findable humorous IRC logs, detailing early Internet culture, which I think are ripped straight from Bash.org, meaning they are real logs written by real people. Stereotypical electronic "hacker" soundtrack which helps the atmosphere of the game.

If any of this interests you, definitely get Hacknet, especially if it's in a bundle or on sale.

I'd advise that anyone with epilepsy be careful with this game at some times - lots of effects are fast or flashy in nature. The story doesn't seem to thrust itself into your face at all. Save for the occasional automated (but justified) email from Bit, you discover all of the story on your own, and every lead and new piece of information feels genuine and is worth discovering. Overall, I had a lot of fun with this game. Two complaints (which end up not really being complaints after I explain them): - The IP map, showing all known devices and their IPs, can get a bit cluttered, and it's easy to forget where one particular computer is on the big web of spinning circles and lines connecting them. The position of an IP address on the map is not always intuitive. However, this could arguably help with immersion, making you feel like you're navigating through a web of IP addresses. It's the internet in its raw form - not catered to your viewing pleasure. - I'm left wanting more. Not that I didn't get my money's worth, but I want more. But that's something every game should strive for - leaving you wanting more, and not outstaying its welcome. Challenging, but *very* rewarding command system that makes you feel clever. Decent story that keeps you invested throughout the game. Findable humorous IRC logs, detailing early Internet culture, which I think are ripped straight from Bash.org, meaning they are real logs written by real people. Stereotypical electronic "hacker" soundtrack which helps the atmosphere of the game. If any of this interests you, definitely get Hacknet, especially if it's in a bundle or on sale.

review_text_raw:
There is no overarching narrative; you're completing puzzles with no purpose. 

Thus, the puzzles are the focus of the game. However, the puzzles are simple and boring. Simple puzzles can still be interesting. Imagine a child's toy where you fit shapes through their respective holes. You can keep yourself busy for a little bit. This game is similar, but everything is a square. How many times can you fit the square in the square hole before it gets boring? Example: you need the password to decrypt a file and you'll find it on the same system within a file called "password.txt". 

Firewall solving requires no input from the player, it's just a timesink. You call the "analyze" command and wait a few seconds at a time until it reveals the answer. You need to call this command multiple times before it starts to reveal the answer - what gameplay function does this serve? Sometimes you don't have any other task to do while the analyze command is processing, so you just wait and wait.. like an idle game. 

Overloading a proxy server involves clicking a button and waiting a few seconds (depending on the number of shells you have up). There's no depth.

Missions share objectives in the form of notes on your computer. For some reason, the devs thought it was a bright idea to have notes take up a significant portion (~30% sometimes) of your memory. So you often have to write up your own abbreviated notes or you won't have enough memory to run the programs you need to crack the ports. The game is fighting itself.

The UI is a mess. A couple hours and your network map becomes an unintelligible mess with no tools to label systems or otherwise organize it. Missions could at least highlight linked servers.

The music is repetitive. Music can make or break a game. In this case, I found myself shutting off music to play my own playlist in the background so I wouldn't be bored to tears while doing all of the waiting the game requires.

review_text_raw:
This game was a great idea with very poor followthrough. You learn two or three tricks to bypass security, have to collect the appropriate scripts to defeat each of the half dozen interfaces, and then boom, you're a legendary hacker. It's all text-based with a super basic linuxy command line interface, which I'm sure makes some people feel like they're all h4xx0r... I'm probably being unnecissarily harsh, but I really was shocked at how repetative this game was. 

It seemed like there were alot of mechanics that they planned, but never got around to implementing. All that hype about deleting the logs after you access a computer... maybe I missed something, but I couldn't see that it did anything. And the Trap and Forkbombs... were those actually useful somehow? Oh, and it was very easy to make game-breaking mistakes, like deleting a file you were supposed to steal. Alot of silent ways to ruin the game and be unable to recover... hope you didn't save after one of those.

There are alot of fun points. Getting a new script and seeing the new computers you can crack is exciting. The story in the beginning and end of the game are interesting. Also the little easter-eggs of emails and chat snippets were pretty funny. And I'm sure the game does look cool if you let people see you playing it. 

My background in embedded sofware may have colored my opinion a bit, but the game felt awfully thin for $10. And from a gameplay perspective, it was awfully rough. Serious programmers should look at TIS-100 instead, although beware: Zacktronics games are not for the faint-hearted, and may feel a little too much like work to the professional programmer.
